facts.statement: The genus Idiacanthus was described by W. K. H. Peters in 1877.
facts.quote: authority: W. K. H. Peters, 1877

facts.statement: Idiacanthus is a genus of barbeled dragonfishes whose larvae exhibit the Stylophthalmine trait.
facts.quote: Idiacanthus is a genus of barbeled dragonfishes, the larvae of which are noted for exhibiting the Stylophthalmine trait.

facts.statement: The name Idiacanthus comes from the Greek words for 'own' and 'spine' or 'thorn'.
facts.quote: Etymology: greek: idia = own, privat + akantha = spine, thorn

facts.statement: There are three recognized species in the genus: Idiacanthus antrostomus, Idiacanthus atlanticus, and Idiacanthus fasciola.
facts.quote: There are currently three recognized species in this genus: Idiacanthus antrostomus C. H. Gilbert, 1890 (Pacific blackdragon) Idiacanthus atlanticus A. B. Brauer, 1906 (Black dragonfish) Idiacanthus fasciola W. K. H. Peters, 1877 (Ribbon sawtail fish)

facts.statement: Members of the genus Idiacanthus live in the mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones.
facts.quote: Members of this genus have been found from the mesopelagic zone to the bathypelagic zone.

facts.statement: Idiacanthus fasciola is widely distributed in the North and South Atlantic, the Indo-Pacific, and other areas.
facts.quote: Idiacanthus fasciola is more widely distributed, found in both North and South Atlantic as well as the Indo-Pacific and other areas.

facts.statement: Idiacanthus antrostomus is mainly found in the Eastern Pacific.
facts.quote: Idiacanthus antrostomus is mainly found in the Eastern Pacific.

facts.statement: A fertile female Idiacanthus fasciola can hold approximately 14,000 eggs.
facts.quote: The average fertile Idiacanthus fasciola female is known to hold approximately 14,000 eggs.

facts.statement: Female Idiacanthus can reach 40 cm in length, while males reach a maximum of 5 cm.
facts.quote: Female idiacanthidae can reach 40 cm in length whereas males have been recorded to only reach a maximum of 5 cm.

facts.statement: Male Idiacanthus lack teeth, a chin barbel, and a functioning gut.
facts.quote: The smaller male has neither teeth, chin barbel, nor a functioning gut.

facts.statement: Both male and female Idiacanthus have small photophores spread throughout their bodies.
facts.quote: Both males and females have small photophores spread throughout the body.

facts.statement: Female Idiacanthus have black skin, while males are dark brown.
facts.quote: Females have black skin while male idiacanthidae are dark brown.

facts.statement: The premaxilla, maxilla, and mandible teeth of Idiacanthidae are almost all capable of being depressed.
facts.quote: Their premaxilla, maxilla, and mandible teeth are almost all capable of being depressed.

facts.statement: Idiacanthidae have pectoral fins in their larval stage but lose them in adulthood.
facts.quote: Idiacanthidae also present pectoral fins in larvae, but have an absence in adulthood.

facts.statement: Idiacanthus have a strip of chevron-shaped luminescent tissue along the dorsal and ventral sides that glows yellow or blue-green when stimulated.
facts.quote: Along both the dorsal and ventral sides of its body, the Idiacanthus has a single strip of chevron-shaped spots of luminescent tissue that, when stimulated, appears to glow either yellow or blue-green.

facts.statement: Studies by William T. O'Day in 1973 showed that Idiacanthus luminescent tissue can be stimulated by adrenaline injection, topical application, seawater solutions with adrenaline, or tactile touch.
facts.quote: Studies by William T. O'Day in 1973 have shown that this tissue can be stimulated by injection of adrenaline into the muscle, topical application of adrenaline, submersion of the body in a solution of sea water and adrenaline, and occasionally tactile touch.

facts.statement: The duration of the emitted light from Idiacanthus has been observed to last only a few seconds.
facts.quote: The duration of the emitted light has only been observed to be a few seconds long.

facts.statement: Idiacanthus belongs to the family Stomiidae, subfamily Idiacanthinae, order Stomiiformes, and class Actinopterygii.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Actinopterygii superordo: Stenopterygii ordo: Stomiiformes subordo: Phosichthyoidei familia: Stomiidae subfamilia: Idiacanthinae genus: Idiacanthus genus_authority: Peters, 1877

facts.statement: Idiacanthus, known as devil fish or black dragons, are marine fish of the stomiid family distributed in the abyssal waters of all oceans.
facts.quote: Los Idiacanthus, conocidos como peces-demonio o dragones negros, son peces marinos de la familia estómidos, distribuidos por las aguas profundas abisales de todos los océanos.

facts.statement: Idiacanthus are large fish with a described maximum length between 38 and 53 cm.
facts.quote: Tienen tamaño grande, con una longitud máxima descrita entre 38 y 53 cm.

facts.statement: Three species have been described in this genus: Idiacanthus antrostomus (Pacific black dragon), Idiacanthus atlanticus (Atlantic black dragon), and Idiacanthus fasciola (common black dragon).
facts.quote: Se han descrito tres especies en este género: Idiacanthus antrostomus (Gilbert, 1890 ) - Hocicudo o dragón negro del Pacífico Idiacanthus atlanticus (Brauer, 1906) - Dragón negro del Atlántico Idiacanthus fasciola (Peters, 1877) - Dragón negro común

facts.statement: A fossil genus named Idiacanthus by Gunnell in 1933 is classified under Chondrichthyes and lived from the Moscovian to Kasimovian (312.8 to 306 million years ago).
facts.quote: PBDB name: Idiacanthus (genus), Gunnell 1933 Parent group: Selachii Class: Chondrichthyes Time range: Moscovian to Kasimovian (312.8 to 306 million years ago)
